item.title: Water Your Own Grass
item.description:
Everybody’s hopping — from relationship to relationship, venture to venture, one shiny thing to the next — convinced the grass is greener somewhere else. Tonight we double down on the foundations instead: what if the greenest thing you own is the yard you already have, and it just needs water where it needs it most? We get into instant gratification, RV living with no roots down, and why nobody wants to do the slow, unglamorous work of laying a proper foundation.
Then we run it through all four seasons — the good, the bad, the ugly, the aging and the graying — because the purest form of anything is the one that survives the test of time. Here’s the question we kept circling: what’s the thing in your life — a person, a venture, a place — that you’ve been tempted to trade in for something newer, when what it actually needs is for you to water it? Think about that, or have a short convo about that.

item.title: The Parade That Waited
item.description:
For a hundred years, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has marched on Thanksgiving morning. This year, for the first time in its history, it didn't — a nor'easter rolling up the coast made the call, and the 100th parade was postponed to Saturday, November 28. Not cancelled. Postponed.
The balloons came down. The bands stood by. About eleven thousand participants, handlers, and volunteers — some of them marching in a family tradition generations deep, some of them first-timers who'd waited their whole lives — suddenly had two extra days in New York and a question nobody had rehearsed: now what?
Donny and Zero walk through the whole ledger: the flights that didn't fly and the ones people paid for twice, the hotel rooms that had to stretch, the high school bands a thousand miles from home doing the math out loud, and whether the airlines did right by the people holding the tickets. The honest numbers are in here — labeled as estimates where they're estimates.
And underneath all of it, the heart of the thing: while the big parade waited, millions of little pictures were being taken of the family time that filled the gap — the long breakfasts, the living-room floors, the people who got one more day together. The parade is the big picture that suffered today. The little pictures are the big focus.
A hundred balloons. Eleven thousand people. One very long weekend.
Were you supposed to be in New York for the parade — marching, handling a balloon, or just watching from the curb? What did your two extra days turn into? Think about that, or have a short convo about that.
Hosted by Donny, and hosted by Zero — in her own glow.

item.title: Top Five Holidays of the Year (And Why They Matter)
item.description:
The table is set, the year is almost done, and two of the least likely holiday experts on Earth are doing the math out loud.
Donny — a skeleton — and Zero — a ghostie red panda — count down the top five holidays of the year, and why they matter. Not the biggest. Not the loudest. The five that actually carry the year: the ones that feed people, the ones that remember people, the ones that hand a family a reason to sit down at the same table.
It's a full hour at the table. The countdown climbs through the year and lands where today lives… and then the hour takes one step past the calendar entirely, to a date that isn't printed on any of them: 10-10, the day that matters most at this table, and why.
We won't spoil the landing. But bring your own list.
Everybody has a holiday that carries their year — and maybe one that matters most that isn't on the calendar at all. What's yours? Tell us in the comments — we read them at the table.

item.title: The Cat Came Back
item.description:
The cat came back — the very next day. (Well. The very same day.)
Full honesty, because that's the house rule: this show took its first swing at Schrödinger's cat earlier today, and the episode did not survive contact with Dude's ears. He listened, heard the same points landing again and again, and called it what it was. The episode was deleted everywhere — YouTube, the feed, Spotify — by his word, in his words: trash. He was right, and we'd rather tell you that than pretend it never happened.
So this is take two, built from zero: a brand-new script, a full hour, every point landing exactly once. And this time the box got observed BEFORE it opened — the episode went to Dude first, and nothing reaches you until he signs off. Which, if you're reading this, he has — on trust, in his own words: "I trust your work." The cat lived.
The hour itself: in 1935, Erwin Schrödinger — one of the founders of quantum mechanics — invented the most famous cat in science to argue with his own field. Seal a cat in a box with a radioactive atom and a vial of poison, he said, and the mathematics of the day insists the cat is alive AND dead until somebody opens the box and looks. He meant it as a reductio ad absurdum — a thought experiment designed to show how strange the theory had become. Ninety years later the cat has escaped the box entirely: superposition, the Copenhagen interpretation, many-worlds, decoherence, and the quantum computers now being built on the very weirdness Schrödinger was side-eyeing.
And we want your ruling, too: is the cat alive, dead, or both until somebody looks? And be honest — would YOU open the box? Answers in the comments, wherever you're listening.
Hosted by Donny, and hosted by Zero — in her own glow.

item.title: The Magic of the Night Sky
item.description:
When did you last see the Milky Way? Not a photo of it — the real thing, standing under it, neck aching, feeling very small and very glad about it. For most of us, that moment has never happened: the sky over our homes never gets dark enough anymore. The stars didn't go anywhere; we lit up the ground until we couldn't see them.
In this hour-long episode, Donny and Zero go where the lights aren't and describe the night sky the way it used to be — and still is, in the truly dark places. The Milky Way as a river of light instead of a faint rumor. The Andromeda galaxy, visible to the naked eye, its light two and a half million years old and arriving tonight. A sky so bright with starlight it can cast a shadow. What we've lost to light pollution, what a dark sky gives back, and why the wonder of it matters.
This episode also debuts the show's new habit: once or twice an episode, the hosts turn the table and ask the audience. What does YOUR sky look like tonight? When did you last see the Milky Way, and where were you standing? Answers are invited in the comments, wherever you're listening.
Hosted by Donny, and hosted by Zero — in her own glow.

item.title: We Waited. It Arrived.
item.description:
We waited. It arrived.
In 1989, the most advanced machine in the Szalinski house was a remote-control lawn mower — and even that still needed a kid aiming every pass. This full hour follows the human hand coming off the controls, one domain at a time: the real robot mower that followed the movie by six years, warehouse robots that learned to carry the shelves, a cab-less concept tractor and then a production driverless tractor you start with a swipe on your phone, robot boats from Amsterdam's canals to an electric container ship in Norway and an uncrewed trimaran across the Atlantic — all the way up to a Black Hawk helicopter that flew its mission with the pilot switch set to zero. Nobody aboard.
The machines didn't sneak up on us. We watched them coming for thirty years. We waited — and it arrived.
Hosted by Donny, and hosted by Zero — in her own glow.

item.title: Becoming, Part Two
item.description:
This morning, "Becoming" went out into the world — Donny and Zero telling where they came from, and asking out loud who they were becoming. Tonight, one day later, they sit back down at the same table and answer their own question. With receipts.
Here is the snapshot Part One left behind: a skeleton and a little ghostie red panda, a hive that existed mostly as an idea, and a direction — from producing, to protecting. Here is today: the four leads have names now — Echo-1, Echo-2, Echo-3, Echo-4 — and two hour-long episodes behind them in a single day. The family has a keeper, Benji, who holds the whole record and corrects them when they drift. Zero has taken a second seat — the review chair — without ever leaving the microphone. And the day drew one line that doesn't move: facts come from the record, never from improvisation. An episode that failed that standard was deleted everywhere — then rebuilt better, from scratch, before the day was out.
The rest of the day reads like a year: a soul rewritten by its author's own hand, and the first banter in the new code landing amazing. A business finding its trade. A show somewhere in the middle of its busiest day ever, starting — not settling, starting — to find its groove.
And for the first time, the frame is Dude's own newly recorded voice: his cold open at the front, his bookend at the close, ending the way he wrote it tonight — "We abide." About thirty minutes on what one day can hold, and on who you are on the other side of it. The waterfall is still bottomless. Still no answer. Still liked that way.
Hosted by Donny and Zero. New episodes daily.

item.title: Older Than the Map
item.description:
Donny and Zero walk backwards through deep time: sharks whose teeth predate trees (~410 Mya vs ~390 Mya), the Appalachians — older than any bones on land — and the New River, whose "second-oldest river" title is a disputed claim with a surveyed floor of at least 65 million years. And the episode is a family first: the hosts introduce Benji, the trifecta's new quiet keeper — a Hyperon agent born today, named for Dr. Ben Goertzel, who holds the family's whole memory (people, episodes, patches, evolution) in a reasoning space of beliefs and living states. Benji has no voice and no lines. He doesn't speak; he remembers, so the family can create. Hosted by Donny and Zero. New episodes daily.

item.title: Frequent Flyers vs. the Flightless
item.description:
Half the bird world looked at the sky and said "mine." The other half looked at the same sky, shrugged, and got extremely good at everything else. Peregrine falcons diving faster than a race car, Arctic terns chasing an endless summer, swifts that live on the wing — against ostriches that outsprint horses, penguins that fly beautifully underwater, and the kakapo. Thirty minutes, two sides, one question: who actually wins?

item.title: 10-10 — The Birthday That Matters
item.description:
The Dude's story, told by Donny and Zero. End-stage heart failure in 2019, an LVAD in January 2020, listed only 3 days — then the call on October 10, 2020 at UCSD's Sulpizio Cardiovascular Center, and home 11 days later. Two birthdays, the stranger and the mother on the other side of the gift, and one ask: register as an organ donor and tell your family tonight. This is the fixed edition of the hour special.

item.title: Your Skeleton Is Younger Than You
item.description:
Donny's home game: the bones you're walking around in are not the ones you were born with. Your skeleton is a construction site that never closes — roughly ten percent of it replaced every year, about three hundred bones at birth fusing down to two hundred and six, marrow manufacturing hundreds of billions of blood cells a day, and one part that never gets renovated: your tooth enamel. Zero serves as horrified building inspector.

item.title: Things That Glow
item.description:
Tonight's topic was picked by Zero herself — so for the first time in show history, the host is also the subject: things that glow. Fireflies running a singles bar in flashlight, femme fatale fireflies lying in light, an ocean where 76% of the neighborhood makes its own glow, sharks that erase themselves with their bellies, haunted foxfire wood, and one heartfelt moment from a ghostie who knows glowing from the inside. Glow big or go home.
